alt: Average clause: a building worth US$80,000 insured for US$60,000 (three quarters) suffers US$20,000 of fire damage; the insurer pays three quarters of the loss, US$15,000, and the under-insured owner bears US$5,000.
caption: Figure: under-insurance, the insurer pays 60,000/80,000 of a US$20,000 loss

alt: Break-even chart for Chipo's backpacks: fixed costs US$6,000, price US$20, variable cost US$12; total cost and revenue cross at 750 backpacks and US$15,000. Loss to the left, profit to the right; at the expected 1,000 backpacks the margin of safety is 250 backpacks.
caption: Figure: Example 1 drawn as a chart (break-even 750 backpacks, margin of safety 250)

alt: Break-even chart for the uniform maker: fixed costs flat at US$4,000; total cost rises from US$4,000 to US$16,000 and revenue from zero to US$20,000 at 2,000 uniforms; the lines cross at 1,000 uniforms and US$10,000. Loss to the left, profit to the right; at 1,500 uniforms the margin of safety is 500 uniforms.
caption: Figure: break-even chart from Example 1 (fixed costs US$4,000, price US$10, variable cost US$6)

alt: The eight main sections of a business plan in order: executive summary, business background, products or services, market research, marketing plan, operations plan, management and people, and the financial plan with start-up costs, forecasts and break-even.
caption: Figure: the main sections of a business plan

alt: Closing bank balances in Thandeka's cash flow forecast: US$750 in July, then an overdraft of US$400 in August when the fridge is bought, and still US$350 overdrawn in September; negative balances are shown in brackets.
caption: Figure: closing balances from Example 1 (brackets mean overdrawn)

alt: Four channels of distribution: producer to consumer directly; producer, retailer, consumer; producer, wholesaler, retailer, consumer; and producer, agent, wholesaler or retailer, consumer. More intermediaries means more mark-ups but wider reach.
caption: Figure: the four main channels of distribution

alt: Services of a commercial bank in four groups: accepting deposits (current, savings, fixed deposit), lending (overdrafts, loans, mortgages and asset finance), making payments (cheques, cards, EFT and RTGS, standing and debit orders, POS) and other services such as foreign exchange and letters of credit.
caption: Figure: the main services of a commercial bank

alt: Trade and cash discount on the cement order: list price US$2,400, less 15% trade discount of US$360 gives US$2,040, less 5% cash discount of US$102 (taken on US$2,040, not on US$2,400) gives US$1,938 if paid within 14 days.
caption: Figure: Example 1, trade discount first, then cash discount on the reduced amount

alt: Stages of economic integration, each including the one below it: a free trade area has free trade between members; a customs union adds a common external tariff; a common market adds free movement of labour and capital; an economic union adds common economic policies or currency.
caption: Figure: the four stages of economic integration

alt: Average cost per bag at the feed mill falls as output grows: US$6.50 at 1,000 bags a month, US$3.30 at 5,000 bags and US$2.40 at 20,000 bags, because bulk buying cuts variable cost and fixed costs are spread over more bags.
caption: Figure: average cost per bag at three outputs (Example 1)

alt: A franchise: the franchisor supplies the brand, recipes, training, manual and national advertising; the franchisee supplies capital, staff and day-to-day running and pays an initial fee and royalties, often a percentage of sales, while following the franchisor's rules.
caption: Figure: what the franchisor and franchisee give each other

alt: Sequence of home-trade documents between buyer and seller: the buyer sends the enquiry and order; the seller replies with quotation, pro forma invoice if needed, advice note, delivery note, invoice, debit or credit notes and a statement; the buyer pays and the seller issues a receipt.
caption: Figure: who sends each document in home trade, in order

alt: Order of documents in a typical import by sea: indent, pro forma invoice with letter of credit arranged, bill of lading with insurance and certificate of origin, shipping documents through the banks with a bill of exchange, then customs declaration and collection of the goods.
caption: Figure: the order in which documents are used in a typical import by sea

alt: The marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion must fit together and fit the target market; product must meet needs, price is the only P that earns revenue, place makes the product easy to find and promotion makes customers aware of it.
caption: Figure: the four Ps of the marketing mix all aimed at the target market

alt: Chart A after the three supervisor posts are removed: the 24 machinists report directly to the operations manager, so the hierarchy falls from 4 to 3 levels and the operations manager's span of control rises from 3 to 24.
caption: Figure: the flatter structure after removing the supervisor level (3 levels, span of 24)

alt: Organisation chart A of Tendai's Uniforms: managing director with four managers (span 4); the operations manager has three supervisors (span 3) and each supervisor has 8 machinists (span 8); four levels of hierarchy in all.
caption: Figure: Chart A, the organisation chart of Tendai's Uniforms (4 levels)

alt: Sales of flavoured water in thousands of bottles over six years: 20, 60, 140, 210, 230 and 232. Sales rise steeply and then level off, so the product is in maturity, close to saturation, and an extension strategy should be planned.
caption: Figure: the flavoured water example, sales rising and then levelling off

alt: Schematic product life cycle: sales against time rise slowly in introduction, steeply in growth, level off in maturity and fall in decline; the stages are separated by dashed lines.
caption: Figure: the four stages of the product life cycle (schematic, no scale)

alt: Tatenda's freezit sales rose by 35 crates each month: 620, 655, 690 and 725 from March to June. Extending the trend with the average change of 35 gives forecasts of 760 crates for July and 795 for August. The vertical axis starts at 600.
caption: Figure: actual sales (March to June) and the forecast for July and August

alt: Chain of production for a loaf of bread: a farmer grows wheat (primary), a miller makes flour and a bakery makes bread (secondary), then transport and a retailer deliver and sell it (tertiary); value is added at every stage and a bank and insurer support the chain.
caption: Figure: the chain of production for a loaf of bread, from primary to tertiary

alt: Stakeholder map: the business sits between internal stakeholders (owners, managers, employees) and external stakeholders (customers, suppliers, lenders, government, local community, competitors), each shown with its main objective, such as profit for owners and prompt payment for suppliers.
caption: Figure: internal and external stakeholders and what each wants

alt: An increase in demand before a public holiday shifts the demand curve right by 40 crates at every price (D1 to D2); the equilibrium moves from US$6 and 80 crates to US$7 and 100 crates, so both price and quantity rise.
caption: Figure: demand rises by 40 crates at every price, moving equilibrium to US$7 and 100 crates

alt: Demand and supply of tomato crates: the curves cross at US$6 and 80 crates. At US$4 demand is 120 and supply 40, a shortage of 80; at US$7 demand is 60 and supply 100, a surplus of 40; so the price moves back to US$6.
caption: Figure: equilibrium at US$6 and 80 crates, with the shortage at US$4 and the surplus at US$7
